current_activity: Dragoon: parachute and glider landings round Le Muy; drop badly scattered by fog; blocking the Argens valley
notes: Event date: 15 August 1944, from about 0430 (Clarke and Smith, ch. 6, pp. 100-101). Event definition: The task force drops before first light on 15 August round Le Muy to block German movement into the beach area along the Argens corridor; fog scatters the drop, but except for Le Muy itself it executes its D-day missions (Clarke and Smith, chs. 5-6). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 5, p. 77: "The 1st Airborne Task Force's main mission was to prevent German movements into the beach area from the direction of Le Muy and Le Luc through the Argens River corridor"; Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 6, p. 104: "However, except for the seizure of Le Muy, the 1st Airborne Task Force had executed its D-day missions"; Wikipedia, 1st Airborne Task Force: "They were to land around the village of Le Muy". Location: Le Muy, Var (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Le Muy; the drop and landing zones lay round it, and many troopers landed far outside them. Location support: Clarke and Smith and Wikipedia name Le Muy as the drop area. Commander: Major General Robert T. Frederick (Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 3).

current_activity: ordered to secure the Seventh Army east flank from the mouth of the Var north to the Larche Pass
notes: Event date: 25 August 1944 (Clarke and Smith, ch. 10: Patch's orders of 25 August). Event definition: Patch's orders of 25 August give the airborne force, still under direct Seventh Army control, the army's east flank from the mouth of the Var near Nice north into the Alps to the Larche Pass (Clarke and Smith, ch. 10). Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 10, p. 172: "For the immediate future Patch's orders of 25 August specified that the airborne force, continuing to operate under the direct control of the Seventh Army, would secure the army's east flank from the mouth of the Var River near Nice, north into the Alps about 60 miles to the Larche Pass". Location: Nice, Alpes-Maritimes (new place), a representative point with a precision of 50 km. Location approximate: representative point (inferred value): the sector ran about 60 miles from the coast to the Larche Pass; the point is its southern end at Nice, so the precision is 50 km and the confidence 0.3. Location support: Clarke and Smith name the mouth of the Var near Nice as the southern end of the sector. Commander: Major General Robert T. Frederick (Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 3).

current_activity: with the 1st Special Service Force holds the southern third of the Franco-Italian Alpine front
notes: Event date: mid-October 1944 (approximate date: Clarke and Smith, ch. 20, "As of mid-October"). Event definition: In mid-October the French hold about two-thirds of the Alpine front and the task force, including the 1st Special Service Force, the southern third (Clarke and Smith, ch. 20). Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 20, p. 357: "The American 1st Airborne Task Force, including the Canadian-American 1st Special Service Force, held the southern third of the front". Location: Sospel, Alpes-Maritimes (new place), a representative point with a precision of 50 km. Location approximate: representative point (inferred value): Sospel, in the sector the 517th held in September (Wikipedia); the date 15 October stands for mid-October (inferred value). Location support: Clarke and Smith give only the southern third of the front. Commander: Major General Robert T. Frederick (Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 3).

current_activity: task force headquarters dissolved after the airborne units leave the Alpine front
notes: Event date: 23 November 1944 (Wikipedia); about 25 November (Clarke and Smith, ch. 30, n. 32). Event definition: The airborne units begin leaving the Alpine front on 15 November and the task force headquarters is dissolved around the 25th (Clarke and Smith, ch. 30, n. 32); Wikipedia says the task force was sent to Soissons to rest and refit and was disbanded on 23 November, most of its units being attached to the XVIII Airborne Corps. Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 30, p. 581: "The airborne units began departing the Alpine front on 15 November, the 1st Airborne Task Force headquarters was dissolved around the 25th"; Wikipedia, 1st Airborne Task Force: "In November 1944 1ABTF was sent to Soissons to rest and refit, and was disbanded on 23 November 1944". Location: Soissons, Aisne (new place) with a precision of 50 km. Location approximate: Wikipedia sends the task force to Soissons; Clarke and Smith do not say where the headquarters was dissolved, so the confidence is 0.3. Location support: Wikipedia names Soissons. Location caveat: the two sources differ on the date (23 or about 25 November); the earlier, Wikipedia, date is used. Commander: Major General Robert T. Frederick (Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 3).
